---
title: "Finite-horizon ruin: statistical precision and exponential tilting"
subtitle: "Assignment 2b · Numerical investigation"
---

## Question and experimental design

We estimate $p=P(\tau\le100)$ for $S_k=30+\sum_{j=1}^kX_j$ with independent
$X_j\sim U(-1.9,2)$, and $\tau=\inf\{k\ge1:S_k\le0\}$.
The computational question is whether the tilt minimizing variance per trajectory
also minimizes the computing time needed for a given precision. We compare crude
Monte Carlo, full-path importance sampling, and stopped-path importance sampling.
All simulation algorithms live in `project_A/`; the code below organizes experiments.
The horizon is always 100 and initial capital is always 30 unless stated otherwise.

```{r}
#| label: setup
# The Quarto project sets the execution directory to the assignment root.
for (file in c("model.R", "theory.R", "simulation.R", "importance_sampling.R", "experiments.R")) {
  source(file.path("project_A", file))
}
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, digits = 4)
theta_example <- -0.30  # Illustrative tilt; no optimality is assumed.
theta_grid <- seq(-0.65, -0.05, by = 0.05)
```


## Understanding the random walk

The original drift is $E[X]=0.05$, so expected capital increases slightly. Ruin
requires a substantial downward excursion. It is a first-passage event: a path can
cross zero and recover to positive capital by step 100. Consequently,
$\{S_{100}\le0\}\subseteq\{\tau\le100\}$, generally with strict inclusion.

```{r}
#| label: original-paths
#| fig-cap: "Original random walks; color records whether the path ever crosses zero."
set.seed(1101)
original <- simulate_paths(1000)
path_data <- data.frame(path = rep(seq_len(1000), each = 101),
                        time = rep(0:100, 1000),
                        capital = as.vector(t(original$paths)),
                        ruined = rep(is.finite(original$ruin_times), each = 101))
ggplot(path_data, aes(time, capital, group = path, color = ruined)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.18, linewidth = 0.3) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Ruin concerns the whole trajectory", x = "Step", y = "Capital", color = "Ruin") +
  theme_minimal()
knitr::kable(data.frame(paths = 1000,
  ruin_frequency = mean(is.finite(original$ruin_times)),
  nonpositive_final_frequency = mean(original$paths[, 101] <= 0),
  ruined_then_recovered = sum(is.finite(original$ruin_times) & original$paths[, 101] > 0)))
```

These frequencies use only 1,000 paths (seed 1101) for illustration. They are not
our final probability estimates.

## Exponential tilting

Write $M(\theta)=E[e^{\theta X}]=\varphi(\theta)/3.9$ and
$K(\theta)=\log M(\theta)$. Then
$g_\theta(x)=e^{\theta x}/\varphi(\theta)$ on the original support.
Negative $\theta$ shifts mass toward losses. At zero, $\varphi(0)=3.9$ and the
original uniform distribution is recovered. Our implementation uses the centered
support identity $M(\theta)=e^{0.05\theta}\sinh(1.95\theta)/(1.95\theta)$
and series expansions near zero to avoid cancellation.

```{r}
#| label: tilted-densities
#| fig-cap: "Negative tilts assign more density to negative increments."
densities <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1.9, 2, length.out = 400), theta = c(-0.6, -0.3, 0, 0.3))
densities$density <- mapply(tilted_density, densities$x, densities$theta)
ggplot(densities, aes(x, density, color = factor(theta))) + geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Exponential tilt of the increment distribution", x = "Increment", y = "Density", color = expression(theta)) + theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: tilted-paths
#| fig-cap: "Independent path samples under three simulation distributions (seed 1102)."
set.seed(1102)
path_groups <- lapply(c(0, theta_example, -0.55), function(theta) {
  result <- simulate_paths(100, theta)
  data.frame(time = rep(0:100, 100), capital = as.vector(t(result$paths)),
             path = rep(1:100, each = 101), theta = sprintf("theta = %.3f", theta))
})
ggplot(do.call(rbind, path_groups), aes(time, capital, group = path)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "steelblue") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~theta) + labs(title = "Making ruin more typical", x = "Step", y = "Capital") + theme_minimal()
```

Ruin frequencies measured under $g_\theta$ estimate $P_\theta(\tau\le100)$,
not the desired $P(\tau\le100)$. Likelihood ratios correct this change of measure.
All densities are positive on the same support, so the reweighting preserves
unbiasedness.

### Expected capital under different simulation settings

The tilted mean helps explain how the simulation changes: a more negative drift
makes ruin more frequent and may allow paths to stop earlier. These are descriptive
settings, not theoretically selected optima. We select parameters empirically from
variance and timing measurements below and in the performance report.

```{r}
#| label: expected-capital
#| fig-cap: "Expected capital paths for illustrative tilts; optimality is assessed empirically."
expected <- expand.grid(time = 0:100, theta = c(0, theta_example, -0.55))
expected$capital <- 30 + expected$time * tilted_mean(expected$theta)
ggplot(expected, aes(time, capital, color = factor(round(theta, 3)))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Expected capital under alternative tilts", x = "Step", y = "Expected capital", color = expression(theta)) + theme_minimal()
```

## From the mathematical estimators to the R code

### What is one simulated observation?

The time horizon and the Monte Carlo sample size play different roles. In the
mathematics, $n=100$ is the number of possible **time steps**, while $N$ is the
number of independent **trajectories**. In the R interface, the argument `n`
means the number of trajectories, so **R's `n` corresponds to mathematical $N$**;
`horizon` corresponds to mathematical $n$. For example,

```r
estimate_ruin(n = 100000, horizon = 100, theta = theta_example, method = "full")
```

means 100,000 independent paths, each simulated for 100 steps. It does not mean
one path of length 100,000. The default initial capital is 30.

To distinguish increments from estimator contributions, write
$Y^{(i)}=(Y_1^{(i)},\ldots,Y_{100}^{(i)})$ for tilted trajectory $i$ and
$Z_i$ for its single contribution to the estimate. Its capital is
$S_k^{(i)}=30+\sum_{j=1}^kY_j^{(i)}$. Define
$$
A_{100}^{(i)}=\left\{\min_{1\le k\le100}S_k^{(i)}\le0\right\}
             =\{\tau_i\le100\}.
$$
We average **one contribution per trajectory**, including zeros from paths
without ruin. Averaging only over ruined paths would change the estimator and
would generally be biased for the desired probability.

### From a density ratio to a likelihood weight

For one increment, $f(x)=1/3.9$ and
$g_\theta(x)=e^{\theta x}/\varphi(\theta)$ on $[-1.9,2]$.
The individual increments are independent with density $g_\theta$; the joint
density of the vector of its first $m$ increments is
$$
g_{\theta,m}(y_1,\ldots,y_m)
=\prod_{k=1}^m g_\theta(y_k)
=\varphi(\theta)^{-m}\exp\left(\theta\sum_{k=1}^m y_k\right).
$$
Both joint densities are zero outside $[-1.9,2]^m$. On this support,
$$
\begin{aligned}
L_m
&=\frac{f_m(y_1,\ldots,y_m)}{g_{\theta,m}(y_1,\ldots,y_m)}\\
&=\prod_{k=1}^m\frac{1/3.9}{e^{\theta y_k}/\varphi(\theta)}\\
&=\left(\frac{\varphi(\theta)}{3.9}\right)^m
  \exp\left(-\theta\sum_{k=1}^m y_k\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
Rather than multiplying many ratios, the code takes logarithms:
$$
\log L_m
=m\underbrace{\log(\varphi(\theta)/3.9)}_{K(\theta)}
 -\theta\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^m y_k}_{S_m-30}.
$$
This is the exact function used by the simulation, displayed directly from the
loaded module rather than implemented again in this report:

```{r}
#| label: show-log-likelihood-function
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat("```r\nlog_likelihood_ratio <- ",
    paste(deparse(log_likelihood_ratio), collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n", sep = "")
```

Here `steps` is $m$, `log_mgf(theta)` is $K(\theta)$, and `increment_sum` is
$S_m-30$. The function returns **$\log L_m$**, so the simulation subsequently
uses `exp(...)` to recover $L_m$. Although the function name contains “MGF,”
`log_mgf` returns its logarithm, not $M(\theta)$ and not $\log\varphi(\theta)$.
The factor $3.9$ has already been accounted for through $M=\varphi/3.9$.

### The three estimators implemented by `estimate_ruin()`

| Method argument | Distribution of increments | Contribution $Z_i$ | Steps actually simulated |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `"crude"` | Original uniform $f$ | $\mathbf1_{A_{100}^{(i)}}$ | 100 |
| `"full"` | Tilted density $g_\theta$ | $\mathbf1_{A_{100}^{(i)}}L_{100}^{(i)}$ | 100 |
| `"stopped"` | Tilted density $g_\theta$ | $\mathbf1_{A_{100}^{(i)}}L_{T_i}^{(i)}$, $T_i=\min(\tau_i,100)$ | $T_i$ |

In all three cases,
$$
\hat p=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i.
$$
On a ruined path, $T_i=\tau_i$, so the stopped contribution uses $L_{\tau_i}$.
On a path without ruin, $T_i=100$ but the contribution is zero. Writing the weight
as $L_{T_i}$ avoids trying to evaluate $L_\tau$ when $\tau=\infty$.

The crude method sets `theta <- 0`. Then `r_tilted()` generates uniform
increments, $K(0)=0$, and $L_m=\exp(0)=1$. Thus the same weighting code reduces
automatically to the usual zero-or-one indicator. Crude MC is simulated under
$f$, whereas both IS methods simulate under $g_\theta$.

### Reading the actual simulation function

The following is the actual source of `estimate_ruin()` in
`project_A/importance_sampling.R`. Its loop updates many independent paths at
once; each element of its vectors refers to one trajectory. This saves R loop
overhead while preserving the usual step-by-step random-walk construction.

```{r}
#| label: show-estimator-source
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
estimator_source <- readLines(file.path("project_A", "importance_sampling.R"))
estimator_start <- grep("^estimate_ruin <- function", estimator_source)
cat("```r\n", paste(estimator_source[estimator_start:length(estimator_source)],
                         collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n", sep = "")
```

Read the function in four stages:

1. **Initialize the paths.** `capital <- rep(initial_capital, n)` sets all
   $S_0^{(i)}=30$. `times <- rep(Inf, n)` means no crossing has yet been observed.
   This `Inf` is a bookkeeping value, not a claim that the path can never ruin
   after the finite horizon. `steps` stores how many increments were generated.
2. **Generate increments and update capital.** At step `k`,
   `r_tilted(length(active), theta, lower, upper)` draws one independent increment
   for every active path. Adding this vector to `capital[active]` implements
   $S_k^{(i)}=S_{k-1}^{(i)}+Y_k^{(i)}$. `newly_ruined` identifies paths with
   current capital at or below zero and no previously recorded crossing;
   `times[newly_ruined] <- k` therefore records the **first** ruin time.
3. **Choose whether to continue after ruin.** For `"full"` and `"crude"`,
   `active` contains all trajectory indices at every step. They retain their
   recorded ruin time even if they later recover. For `"stopped"`,
   `which(is.infinite(times))` selects only paths without a recorded crossing.
   A ruined path receives no further increments, so its final stored capital
   is $S_\tau$ and its `steps` value is $\tau$.
4. **Construct $Z_i$.** `ruined <- is.finite(times)` represents the event
   indicator. `contributions <- numeric(n)` initializes all $Z_i=0$.
   Only `contributions[ruined]` are replaced by likelihood weights. The argument
   `capital[ruined] - initial_capital` supplies $\sum_{k=1}^mY_k$; `steps[ruined]`
   supplies $m$. These are terminal sums and $m=100$ for full paths, and sums
   through ruin and $m=\tau$ for stopped paths. Finally,
   `summarize_contributions()` averages all $N$ contributions.

| Mathematical object | R variable or expression |
|:--|:--|
| Number of independent trajectories $N$ | `n` |
| Horizon $n=100$ | `horizon` |
| Current $S_k^{(i)}$, or frozen $S_{\tau_i}^{(i)}$ after stopping | `capital[i]` |
| First observed ruin time $\tau_i\le100$ | `times[i]`; otherwise `Inf` |
| $\mathbf1_{\{\tau_i\le100\}}$ | `as.numeric(ruined[i])` |
| Number of simulated increments $m_i$ | `steps[i]` |
| $\sum_{k=1}^{m_i}Y_k^{(i)}$ | `capital[i] - initial_capital` after the loop |
| $Z_i=\mathbf1_{\{\tau_i\le100\}}L_{m_i}$ | `contributions[i]` |
| $\hat p=N^{-1}\sum_iZ_i$ | `mean(contributions)` |

### Worked path: ruin followed by recovery

For a transparent numerical example only, reduce initial capital to 2 and the
horizon to 4. Consider increments $(-0.8,-1.4,1.0,0.6)$ and tilt $\theta=-0.3$.
This is a deterministic example of the calculation, not an estimate of the
original 100-step ruin probability.

```{r}
#| label: worked-path-capital
example_increments <- c(-0.8, -1.4, 1.0, 0.6)
example_capital <- 2 + c(0, cumsum(example_increments))
example_tau <- ruin_times(matrix(example_increments, nrow = 1), initial_capital = 2)[1]
knitr::kable(data.frame(step = 0:4, increment = c(NA, example_increments),
                        capital = example_capital), digits = 3)
```

Ruin occurs at step **`r example_tau`**, although final capital is
**`r tail(example_capital, 1)`**. Thus the indicator is one for both IS methods.
The full method keeps all four increments; the stopped method uses only the
first two. The next table computes each weight both from the formula for
$\log L_m$ and by directly multiplying the one-increment density ratios.

```{r}
#| label: worked-path-weights
example_theta <- -0.3
example_steps <- c(4, example_tau)
example_sums <- c(sum(example_increments), sum(example_increments[seq_len(example_tau)]))
example_log_weights <- log_likelihood_ratio(example_sums, example_steps, example_theta)
example_density_ratios <- c(
  prod(uniform_density(example_increments) / tilted_density(example_increments, example_theta)),
  prod(uniform_density(example_increments[seq_len(example_tau)]) /
         tilted_density(example_increments[seq_len(example_tau)], example_theta)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(method = c("Full", "Stopped"), steps = example_steps,
                        increment_sum = example_sums, log_weight = example_log_weights,
                        contribution = exp(example_log_weights),
                        direct_density_ratio = example_density_ratios), digits = 6)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(exp(example_log_weights), example_density_ratios)))
```

The two columns agree because they evaluate the same density ratio in different
ways. A weight, and hence an individual IS contribution, can exceed one; it is
not itself a probability. On a path with no ruin the contribution would instead
be zero, irrespective of its likelihood weight. For crude MC this ruined path
would contribute one. The full and stopped weights need not agree for an
individual path: their **expectations** agree with the target probability.

### From individual contributions to the reported estimate and standard error

For independent contributions $Z_1,\ldots,Z_N$, the output quantities are
$$
\hat p=\bar Z,\qquad
s_Z^2=\frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(Z_i-\bar Z)^2,\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat p)=\frac{s_Z^2}{N},\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{s_Z^2}{N}}.
$$
Here `var(contributions)` calculates $s_Z^2$, the estimated variance of **one
trajectory's contribution**, whereas `var(contributions) / n` estimates the
variance of the **average**. This distinction accounts for the factor $N$.
The relative standard error is $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}/\hat p$.

The small diagnostic run below exposes the actual contributions returned by the
reusable function. Twelve paths are enough to explain the calculation, but far
too few for the final statistical investigation.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-individual-contributions
set.seed(1201)
diagnostic_run <- estimate_ruin(n = 12, theta = theta_example, method = "stopped",
                                 diagnostics = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(trajectory = 1:12,
                        ruin_time = diagnostic_run$ruin_times,
                        simulated_steps = diagnostic_run$steps,
                        contribution = diagnostic_run$contributions), digits = 6)
```

```{r}
#| label: reconstruct-estimate
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  calculation = c("mean(contributions)", "var(contributions)",
                  "var(contributions) / N", "sqrt(var(contributions) / N)"),
  value = c(mean(diagnostic_run$contributions), var(diagnostic_run$contributions),
            var(diagnostic_run$contributions) / 12,
            sqrt(var(diagnostic_run$contributions) / 12))), digits = 8)
knitr::kable(diagnostic_run$summary[, c("estimate", "contribution_variance",
                                       "estimator_variance", "standard_error")], digits = 8)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mean(diagnostic_run$contributions),
                          diagnostic_run$summary$estimate)))
```

The manually reconstructed values match the returned summary. In contrast,
`ruin_frequency` is `mean(is.finite(ruin_times))`: under a nonzero tilt it
estimates $P_\theta(\tau\le100)$, **not** the weighted target $p$.
The final experiments below use much larger samples and approximate 95% normal
intervals $\hat p\pm1.96\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}$ without truncation. Such intervals
can be unreliable when ruin observations or representative weighted observations
are too few; the tiny diagnostic example is not used for final inference.

### Why both importance sampling estimators are unbiased

For a full path, change of measure gives
$$
E_\theta[Z_F]
=\int\mathbf1_{A_{100}}(y)\frac{f_{100}(y)}{g_{\theta,100}(y)}
 g_{\theta,100}(y)\,dy
=\int\mathbf1_{A_{100}}(y)f_{100}(y)\,dy=p.
$$
The stopped estimator has the same expectation for a different reason than
merely replacing 100 by a shorter path length: its stopping time depends on the
observed increments, and that dependence must be respected.

Set $T=\tau\wedge100$. Under $P_\theta$, the likelihood process is a martingale
because each next density ratio has expectation
$E_\theta[f(Y)/g_\theta(Y)]=1$. On a ruined path, the remaining full-path weight
is a product of independent future density ratios with conditional mean one.
On a non-ruined path, both contributions are zero. Therefore,
$$
E_\theta[Z_F\mid\mathcal F_T]=Z_S.
$$
Taking expectations proves $E_\theta[Z_S]=p$. This conditional-expectation
identity also makes the stopped contribution a Rao–Blackwellization of the full
contribution. By the law of total variance,
$$
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(Z_F)
=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(Z_S)
 +E_\theta[\operatorname{Var}_\theta(Z_F\mid\mathcal F_T)]
\ge\operatorname{Var}_\theta(Z_S).
$$
Thus stopping removes post-ruin likelihood noise without changing the target.
This ordering holds at any **common** tilt; it does not force the two variance
curves to have the same minimizing tilt, nor does it guarantee that every pair
of noisy empirical variances will be ordered.

## Pilot selection and sensitivity

The grid covers moderate through strong negative tilts, from -0.65 to -0.05
in steps of 0.05. Independent simulations at each grid point use seed 2101, with 5,000
and 20,000 paths. The 20,000-path pilot chooses the smallest empirical
contribution variance separately for each estimator. This is a grid search, not
an assertion about a continuous global optimum.

```{r}
#| label: pilot-variance
#| fig-cap: "Variance of an individual weighted contribution across candidate tilts."
pilot <- variance_experiment(theta_grid, c(5000, 20000), seed = 2101)
selected <- select_theta(subset(pilot, n == 20000))
ggplot(pilot, aes(theta, contribution_variance, color = method)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_y_log10() + labs(title = "Variance sensitivity to tilt and pilot size", x = expression(theta),
                         y = "Contribution variance (log scale)") + theme_minimal()
knitr::kable(selected[, c("method", "theta", "contribution_variance")], row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: ruin-frequency
#| fig-cap: "Ruin frequency under the simulation law, estimated with 20,000 paths per point."
ggplot(subset(pilot, n == 20000), aes(theta, ruin_frequency, color = method)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Stronger negative tilts make ruin frequent", x = expression(theta), y = "Simulation ruin frequency") + theme_minimal()
```

Selecting the lowest noisy point creates selection optimism. Flat minima,
grid resolution, and occasionally large likelihood contributions can make the
selected parameter unstable. Agreement across these two sizes is only a limited
sensitivity check. Repeated pilots or a finer local grid would strengthen the
claim; extremely negative tilts are especially vulnerable to unstable second-moment
estimates. A strong tilt making almost every path ruin is not automatically efficient.

## Independent final evaluation

We now discard the pilot samples for evaluation and use seed 2201 with 100,000
new trajectories for each configuration. The fixed illustrative tilt (-0.30) and
pilot-selected tilts are evaluated separately, even if their values coincide.
The common fixed tilt permits a direct full-versus-stopped comparison. Standard errors below describe final
Monte Carlo uncertainty conditional on the chosen parameters, not pilot-selection
uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: final-estimation
set.seed(2201)
configurations <- data.frame(method = c("crude", "full", "stopped", "full", "stopped"),
  choice = c("Original", "Fixed example", "Fixed example", "Pilot variance minimum", "Pilot variance minimum"),
  theta = c(0, theta_example, theta_example,
            selected$theta[selected$method == "full"], selected$theta[selected$method == "stopped"]))
final_rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(configurations)), function(i) {
  cbind(configurations[i, ], estimate_ruin(100000, configurations$theta[i], configurations$method[i])$summary)
})
final <- do.call(rbind, final_rows)
knitr::kable(final[, c("method", "choice", "theta", "estimate", "standard_error", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")], digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(final[, c("method", "choice", "contribution_variance", "estimator_variance", "relative_standard_error", "ruin_frequency")], digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: final-precision
#| fig-cap: "Independent final estimates with approximate 95% Monte Carlo intervals."
final$configuration <- paste(final$method, final$choice, sep = ": ")
ggplot(final, aes(estimate, configuration)) + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper), orientation = "y", width = 0.15) +
  labs(title = "Equal-size final simulations", x = "Ruin probability", y = NULL) + theme_minimal()
```

## Interpretation

The selected grid minima are
**`r round(selected$theta[selected$method == "full"], 4)`** for full paths and
**`r round(selected$theta[selected$method == "stopped"], 4)`** for stopped paths.
These are empirical optima for the tested grid. Nearby values should not be treated
as meaningfully different without stronger simulation evidence.

At the common illustrative tilt (-0.30), the final empirical full/stopped variance ratio is
**`r round(final$contribution_variance[2] / final$contribution_variance[3], 2)`**.
Relative to crude MC, stopped IS at its selected tilt has a contribution-variance
reduction factor of **`r round(final$contribution_variance[1] / final$contribution_variance[5], 2)`**.
Importance sampling improves precision by observing useful ruin trajectories more
frequently and reweighting them correctly. Excessively strong tilting can instead
produce highly uneven weights. Stopping removes irrelevant post-ruin weight
variation through conditional expectation, and also saves increments. The exact
variance ordering does not imply the two variance curves have identical minima.
The companion report evaluates whether saved increments translate to lower
wall-clock cost and whether that changes the preferred tilt.

## Reproducibility

Seeds: 1101 (original paths), 1102 (tilted paths), 2101 (pilot), 2201 (final).
The tables state sample sizes; no saved interactive objects are required.

```{r}
#| label: session-information
sessionInfo()
```
